name: Rósahjálmur
powers: Protects the bearer so that no harm can come to them while it is worn.
description: Rósahjálmur, the rose-helmet of the Huld manuscript, a protection stave said to make the bearer safe from any harm so long as it was worn. Its name suggests a floral or Christian-influenced design unlike the angular battle staves. It is one of the more intricate of the defensive galdrastafir recorded in the grimoires.

name: Rune Calendar
powers: Read like a perpetual printed almanac of the church year.
description: A rune calendar (runkalender or runstav), a perpetual almanac carved on a long wooden or horn staff, used in Sweden from the Middle Ages into the nineteenth century. Each year's structure was fixed with runes: one rune row marked the weekdays, another the golden numbers that place the movable feasts. The staff was read like a printed calendar and was long carried by Swedish farmers and seafarers.
source: Museum collections of rune calendars (e.g. Nordiska museet)

name: The Rök Runestone
maker: Raised by Varin in memory of his son
description: The Rök stone (Rökstenen), the famous ninth-century runestone of Östergötland, raised beside Lake Vättern in memory of a dead son. Its long inscription, the longest known runic text, is a riddling composition mentioning Theodoric the Great, runes, and heroic legend. The Rök stone is one of the most studied objects of Swedish Viking-age runology.

name: Raven Banner
material: Woven wool or silk with a raven device
powers: Was said to flap its wings before victory and hang limp before defeat.
description: A battle standard woven in the shape of a raven, carried by Viking commanders to signal the presence of a great leader. The Orkneyinga saga tells of Earl Sigurd's banner Landeyðan, said to predict victory by flapping its wings, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records a raven banner among Danish Vikings in 878. The raven was Odin's bird, making the banner a war-charm as much as a flag.

name: The Red Shoes
powers: The shoes make their wearer dance, without rest, wherever she goes.
description: The enchanted red shoes of Andersen's tale of Karen, a proud village girl who wants shoes finer than her station. Once she puts on the red shoes they carry her dancing uncontrollably, over thorns and across the country, until she has the axe cut them from her feet and repents. The tale, rooted in village dress codes, made fine shoes a symbol of vanity punished.
source: Hans Christian Andersen, De røde sko (1845)

name: The Roskilde Ships
description: Five Viking-age ships raised in 1962 from the mouth of Roskilde Fjord, where they had been scuttled to block the channel. The fleet holds a deep-sea cargo knarr, a Baltic trader, and two long warships, showing the whole range of Viking shipbuilding. They are displayed in the Viking Ship Museum at Roskilde, where the longship Skuldelev 2 was rebuilt at full scale.

name: Rooster of Barcelos
material: Legendary roast fowl; modern ceramic replicas
powers: A roasted rooster rose and crowed to prove a condemned pilgrim's innocence.
description: The Rooster of Barcelos, from the Portuguese legend of a Galician pilgrim wrongly condemned to hang in Barcelos; before the judge, the pilgrim swore his innocence by the roasted rooster on the table, and the bird rose and crowed. The miracle saved him, and the ceramic Galo de Barcelos became a national symbol.
source: Portuguese oral tradition; collected versions of the Barcelos legend

name: The Round Table
powers: Seated all the knights of Arthur's court without quarrels over precedence.
description: The Round Table of King Arthur, the great table at which none of the knights could claim a higher seat than another. In Geoffrey of Monmouth it is a table of guests; in later romance the table, like Arthur's court, is divided when Merlin reads the fate of a knight who will win the Grail. A 13th-century table at Winchester is linked to the legend.
source: Geoffrey of Monmouth; Arthurian romance; Winchester table

name: Rostam's Spear
powers: The heavy lance carried beside the mace and lasso in the hero's trials.
description: The heavy war-spear of the hero Rostam in the Shahnameh, carried alongside his bull-headed mace and lasso through the Haft Khan and the wars against Turan, and used to strike down champions in single combat. In Ferdowsi's epic it is one of the enormous plain weapons that suit his strength, wielded in duels such as the fateful fight with Sohrab. Its details follow epic convention.

name: The Ruby of Qabus
aliases: Ruby of the Tower of Qabus
powers: A treasure gem of the Ziyarid ruler's court.
description: A great ruby linked in Persian legend and anecdote with Qabus, the Ziyarid ruler and patron of scholars remembered for the tower tomb of Gonbad-e Qabus. The gem is said to have been kept among his treasures or set in his regalia, but no named early source describes it in any detail, and the surviving references belong to later literary tradition. Its particulars therefore cannot be verified.

name: Ruyi Jingu Bang
powers: Shrinks and grows at the wearer's will; weighs thirteen thousand five hundred catties
description: The magic staff of Sun Wukong the Monkey King, pulled from the East Sea Dragon Palace where it stood as a pillar weighing thirteen thousand five hundred catties. It shrank and grew at its bearer's will, and its gold-banded ends helped the Monkey King defy the heavenly host before he was pressed into escorting the pilgrim Tripitaka to the West.

name: Rewe
material: Carved wooden post with notched steps
powers: Ladder by which the machi climbs to speak with the spirits.
description: The tall notched post raised at the center of Mapuche ceremonies, its steps climbed by the machi to draw close to the upper world of the spirits; the rewe marks the place where the sacred and human worlds meet. Each rewe is carved and planted with ceremony, often with images of the beings that guide the machi. It stands at the heart of the ngillatun ritual ground.
source: Mapuche oral tradition and ethnographic studies
